canberra.title: WATCH: Metro servos raided over illicit tobacco sales
canberra.snippet: Police have raided Metro Petroleum service stations across Australia, including in the ACT, and seized illegal tobacco and vapes the serv...
canberra.content:
The raids were carried out at more than 100 locations around the country. Image: Screenshot.

Police have raided Metro Petroleum service stations across Australia, including in the ACT, and seized illegal tobacco and vapes the servos have been allegedly selling.

The Illicit Tobacco National Disruption Group (ITNDG) coordinated a large-scale, multi-jurisdictional operation on Tuesday (11 August) across the ACT, NSW, Queensland, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia, targeting the sale of illicit tobacco and vapes.

Metro Petroleum is one of Australia’s largest independent service station operators but has little presence in either Tasmania or the Northern Territory, so those jurisdictions were not included in the raids.

Known as Operation Shorthand, the joint effort simultaneously targeted more than 100 servos across the country.

A multi-agency taskforce has raided Metro Petroleum servos across Australia, including this one in Phillip, ACT. Photo: ABF

The coordinated effort involved the Australian Border Force, Australian Federal Police, Access Canberra, ACT Policing, Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, Therapeutic Goods Administration, NSW Police Force, NSW Crime Commission, and the health and police departments of other states, as well as some jurisdictional tobacco licensing and consumer authorities.

All up, about 250 law enforcement and regulatory officers from 15 agencies were deployed across the country.

There are half a dozen Metro servos across the ACT with a couple more in Queanbeyan. It is unclear how many were visited during the operation, with the Australian Border Force refusing to confirm the number when asked.

It did, however, release vision of the raid on the Metro servo in Phillip.

Operation Shorthand was established following an intelligence referral into the ITNDG by the AFP and the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, identifying alleged links between the service stations, suspected criminal activity and the alleged sale of illicit tobacco and vapes.

The operation remains active, with the ITNDG and partner agencies continuing to assess materials and information gathered during enforcement activities.

No charges have been laid yet.

Decisions over whether to close the service stations are left to relevant state and territory agencies under each jurisdiction’s legislation.

In determining any closure action, these agencies carefully considered a range of operational and community factors, including the location of the premises and the availability of fuel and essential services for local consumers.

Agencies will announce official outcomes from the operation next week.

Assistant Customs Minister Julian Hill has a message for traders in illegal tobacco: “We’re coming after you.”

Federal Assistant Minister for Citizenship and Customs, Julian Hill, called a snap media conference at Parliament House to announce the raids and thank all agencies involved.

He confirmed that only one service station brand was targeted in the national raids, but said more outlets selling illicit tobacco products are likely to be caught up in further enforcement exercises.

“The message to anyone involved in the illegal tobacco trade is this — we’re coming after you,” Mr Hill said.

“Australians wouldn’t put up with a meth lab in the middle of their local strip shopping centre and neither should they put up with crooks trying to sell tobacco and nicotine products to their kids – whether it’s from a shop, servo, pub or a barber.”

Metro Petroleum has issued a general statement acknowledging police attendance at some of their Metro-branded stations across the country, which it says it welcomes.

The company has strongly denied any involvement in the selling of illegal tobacco and the owners are not accused of any wrongdoing.

“Metro will cooperate fully with the Australian Border Force, the Australian Federal Police, NSW Police and every other agency involved, and with any investigation or government-led initiative directed at removing the illicit tobacco trade or any operator said to be breaking the law,” the statement said.

“Metro has a zero-tolerance approach to the sale of illicit tobacco and vaping products.

“Metro rejects, without qualification, any suggestion that it knew of, permitted, profited from, or was in any way involved in the sale of illicit tobacco or in any supply chain for illicit tobacco.”

The ITNDG was established in October last year and is a multi-agency group led by the Australian Border Force to complement the Illicit Tobacco Taskforce, which targets serious and organised criminal networks in the illicit tobacco market.

The Federal Government promotes the ITNDG as a “first-of-its-kind approach” in disrupting mid-level criminals and enablers in the illicit tobacco market, bringing together traditional and non-traditional agencies in a “whole-of-government capability” model.

canberra.title: ‘Fear and intimidation’: Wagga Council threatens to fine Wilks Park homeless
canberra.snippet: Wagga Council has threatened to fine homeless people living in makeshift tents at Wilks Park if they do not leave the site, prompting acc...
canberra.content:
11 August 2026

Start the conversation

Police officers and Wagga Council workers move through the campsite issuing letters. Photo: Supplied.

Wagga Council has threatened to fine homeless people living in makeshift tents at Wilks Park if they do not leave the site, prompting accusations the council is using “fear and intimidation” against some of the city’s most vulnerable residents.

Council compliance officers, accompanied by four police officers, visited the park on Tuesday (11 August) and issued dozens of letters to people living at the camp because they have nowhere else to live.

The letter told residents they were not permitted to camp in the area and had to vacate the site by Tuesday, 25 August.

Anyone who failed to comply with the notice was “guilty of an offence”, with the council holding the “power to issue a penalty notice [fine] for non-compliance”.

Housing advocate Vickie Burkinshaw said the action was a cruel response to people already facing considerable uncertainty.

“This is fear and intimidation to our most vulnerable and it’s something we should all be ashamed of,” she said.

“Once again, all our effort is going towards compliance — if we have the time and resources to send police officers and council workers to the camp, why don’t we have the time and resources to help them?”

Advocates who observed the compliance action said council workers and police were respectful and polite, but argued it represented a backflip from the more compassionate approach they believed the council had agreed to just two weeks earlier.

“Our understanding was no enforceable action until September, to give Homes NSW the time needed to house people,” Ratepayers Association president Chris Roche said.

“We had hoped that council was going to take a more compassionate approach moving forward … but this shows the cruelty of council to people that are vulnerable.”

Wagga Council defended the action in a statement issued on Tuesday.

“The letter has been issued after council was informed that the rough sleepers had been given misleading information that suggested council was not going to exercise regulatory powers,” a spokesperson said.

“The letter details the conditions of staying at the park, what powers council has in enforcing these conditions, and also details the support services that are available to anyone who needs them.

“Wilks Park is a primitive campground, with a 72-hour limit and basic facilities meant for the community and for people travelling through Wagga Wagga as a short-term location where they can stay in their own self-contained accommodation such as campers or caravans. It is not designed as a place for someone to stay in a tent or other temporary accommodation for prolonged periods.”

The council said it had so far chosen not to undertake compliance action against anyone experiencing homelessness in Wagga Wagga and would continue to take this approach where people were actively engaging with support services to access more suitable accommodation.

But advocates say the people being ordered out of the park have nowhere else to go.

They say a lack of social housing means many homeless people are instead being directed into hotel rooms, which the advocates argue are not a sustainable alternative.

“Moving from one hotel room to another is not a viable option for someone trying to rebuild their life,” Ms Burkinshaw said.

“There aren’t enough in Wagga. I heard some homeless were moved out of their rooms during the NRLW Magic Round, when we had an influx of visitors.

“If you are stuck into a hotel room that has no way to cook for yourself, and you can’t have visitors, what do you do? We are further isolating people who need community support.”

Former ABC journalist Moyra Shields said the new approach represented the worst of both worlds.”We have privatised the homeless industry,” she said.

“We are paying private operators who own motels to house the homeless because we’re not building enough public housing. It doesn’t make sense because taxpayers are paying so much more — it also pushes up prices of hotel rooms for the rest of us.”

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: Australian native birds to be vaxxed against bird flu
canberra.snippet: Vaccines against H5 bird flu will be rolled out for Australia’s native bird species population, with the priority being placed on animals...
canberra.content:
Native bird species in captivity will be given vaccines against H5 bird flu. Photo: File

Vaccines against H5 bird flu will be rolled out for Australia’s native bird species population, with the priority being placed on animals in captivity.

Targeted trials have already taken place and attention is now turning to broadening the effort as the latest strain of the deadly virus spreads across the country.

There are now more than 230 detections of H5 in wild birds in Australia, with affected birds having been found in NSW, South Australia, Western Australia, Victoria and Queensland.

Environment Minister Murray Watt said on Tuesday (11 August) birds will need two vaccines to be more thoroughly protected against the virus, but biosecurity measures will also need to be beefed up to protect vulnerable species and help stop the spread.

“Where it is possible to vaccinate wild birds we will do so, but the priority is to vaccinate birds that are in captivity and in zoos and other institutions,” the Minister said.

“We have been taking steps to ensure we do have populations of our most vulnerable bird species and they are going to be the priority when it comes to vaccination.

“This announcement to broaden out our vaccination program is another step to protect our native birds, and that builds on the steps that we have already taken over the last couple of years.”

The Federal Government has increased captive breeding programs in zoos to build up viable populations of the most endangered species.

It forms part of the government’s $113 million bird flu preparedness plan, which has also included sealing zoo enclosures to prevent wild birds entering.

Senator Watt described the spread of the virus in Australia as a serious, escalating situation.

Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said about 1500 vials of the vaccine had been secured at a cost of more than $2 million.

She said the Federal Government will work with the states and territories, which have all been testing the vaccines on birds to see which respond best.

State and territory governments will announce which bird populations in their jurisdictions will get the vaccines first.

“I can announce that the first vaccines are expected to roll out in coming days and weeks based on an agreed national approach to the targeted vaccination of priority native bird species,” Ms Collins said.

“This approach will mean that the states and territories are able to commence vaccination activities, initially focusing on priority species in captivity identified by those states and territories.

“We’ve been very clear that we cannot stop the H5 bird flu from spreading amongst wild birds … Australians should expect to see more spread and larger numbers, particularly of dead birds and mass mortalities around the country from the H5 bird flu.

“We have been very clear that this will continue to spread across the country.”

The Agriculture Minister said there was still no evidence that the bird flu strain had infiltrated Australia’s poultry and agricultural sectors.

During Question Time in the House of Representatives later in the day, Ms Collins gave a state-by-state breakdown of the bird flu numbers detected to date, which total 236.

Shadow agriculture minister Darren Chester rose to thank the minister for her efforts and for engaging with the Opposition on the issue.

He promised a continuing bipartisan approach to responding to the bird flu in Australia.

Earlier, chief veterinary officer Beth Cookson told the media that while she was confident Australia had enough vaccines to meet initial requirements, other measures needed to be maintained.

“There are some limitations in terms of the way the vaccine can be used, including the vials needing to be disposed of after being opened,” she said.

“We have been working very carefully for the last 18 months as part of our national preparedness to make sure that we have safety and efficacy data available to us as to appropriate vaccines to use in captive and managed populations.

“It is not a stand-alone solution, bio security will remain important, the protection of these species.”

canberra.title: Major cocaine yacht seizure leads to confiscation of $300,000
canberra.snippet: An investigation that allegedly found millions of dollars’ worth of cocaine hidden inside a Queensland yacht has now resulted in th...
canberra.content:
11 August 2026

Police allegedly seized almost $300,000 in cash during a raid in Canberra in 2023. Photo: AFP.

An investigation that allegedly found millions of dollars’ worth of cocaine hidden inside a Queensland yacht has now resulted in the confiscation of about $300,000 cash that was seized during a raid in Canberra.

In July 2023, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) alleged 247 kg of cocaine had been discovered inside a yacht that had arrived in Townsville after sailing from Vanuatu.

Police originally estimated this cocaine had a street value of almost $62 million.

It was alleged two men from Canberra, then aged 44 and 55, had travelled to Townsville earlier that year to try to recover the drugs.

When police raided an apartment in Griffith in the ACT, one of the men allegedly threw a backpack containing $290,000 cash from the balcony.

“The seized cash was alleged payment for assisting in the cocaine importation,” an AFP spokesperson said.

The two men, now aged 47 and 58, were handed charges of possessing a commercial quantity of unlawfully imported border controlled drugs and they remain before the courts in Queensland.

An AFP spokesperson said their investigation could not establish a legitimate source or explanation for the seized cash.

The money was restrained under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 in 2025. Then, in August 2026, police obtained forfeiture orders in the District Court of Queensland regarding the cash and it was formally confiscated.

The AFP spokesperson said the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 allows police to restrain and forfeit proceeds of crime based on a civil standard of proof.

The funds are then used to benefit the community through crime prevention, intervention or diversion programs, or other law enforcement initiatives.

AFP Commander Andrea Quinn said police continued to target proceeds of crime through forfeitures.

“The Proceeds of Crime Act provides law enforcement with important powers to identify, restrain and forfeit assets connected to alleged criminal activity,” she said.

“Confiscating criminal wealth is essential to preventing offenders from benefiting from their unlawful conduct, and by depriving criminals of their profits we reduce their capacity to finance further offending.

“That is why the AFP works closely with its partners in the Criminal Assets Confiscation Taskforce to target illicit wealth and ensure confiscated funds are redirected for the benefit of the Australian community.”

canberra.title: Remorseless rapist rages at chief justice in dramatic end to sentencing
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual assault and family violence. During a horrific three-day ordeal, a woman was terrorised an...
canberra.content:
A 44-year-old man was sentenced to a total of eight-and-a-half years’ jail over abusing his ex-partner. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to sexual assault and family violence.

During a horrific three-day ordeal, a woman was terrorised and traumatised by her violent ex-partner when he repeatedly assaulted, raped and humiliated her.

But even though the man learned he only had to stay in jail for an extra few weeks over this abuse, he still flew into an abusive tirade against the ACT Supreme Court’s top judge when he was sentenced.

The 44-year-old had already spent over nine-and-a-half years in jail due to other crimes before he was sentenced on Tuesday (11 August) for abusing the woman.

Due to this lengthy time in custody, Chief Justice Lucy McCallum said he would become eligible for parole in November 2026.

The man’s defence lawyer then said he was instructed to seek a suppression order over her entire judgement, which outlined the reasons for her decision and his client’s crimes.

“No, I won’t do that,” Chief Justice McCallum replied.

The man soon started yelling and swearing from the courtroom’s dock.

“I got stabbed 15 times in the f-ing jail,” he said.

Chief Justice McCallum told him to “stop swearing” and told custodial officers to keep him in the courtroom when they tried to take him out as he was continuing to yell over the top of her.

“You f-ing listen to what I’m f-ing saying,” the man told the judge.

He then grabbed a water bottle and appeared to start to throw it before three custodial officers intervened and tried to restrain him, resulting in a struggle as he fought against them.

“Let me out, please,” he yelled.

“I can’t breathe.”

After the man was taken out of the courtroom, Chief Justice McCallum told his defence lawyer that his client’s outburst had demonstrated how, contrary to what he had told people, he had not learned to control his anger and had not learned to not shout at women who annoyed him.

“He better get on top of that before he applies for parole,” she told the lawyer.

Earlier, Chief Justice McCallum said the woman’s three-day ordeal began in 2011 when she woke up to the man stomping on her head.

He spat on her, dragged her around and used a Stanley knife to slash at her groin.

The man refused to let her wear clothes, wouldn’t let her use the bathroom, forced her to urinate in the backyard then kicked her to the ground when she did so, and refused to let her drink or eat.

He also raped her four times, including while spitting on her and insulting her.

The court heard the man was addicted to meth at the time and believed the woman had been unfaithful to him.

After two jury trials, the man was found guilty of four counts of sexual intercourse without consent, two acts of indecency-related charges and one count of assault. He pleaded guilty to a second assault charge, while the chief justice found him guilty of two more.

Chief Justice McCallum said he had shown no remorse for his offences.

The man, who has not been named to avoid identifying the woman, was sentenced to a total of eight-and-a-half years’ jail, backdated to his arrest on these family violence charges and ending in November 2031.

He has been in custody since November 2016 over previous offending, and his sentences for these crimes were scheduled to end in October 2026. As a result, Chief Justice McCallum said it was appropriate he only spend a total of 10 years in jail, partly due to the risk of becoming institutionalised.

She reset his non-parole period to allow him to apply for parole from November 2026.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Canberra Rape Crisis Centre on 02 6247 2525, the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 02 6280 0900, the Sexual Violence Legal Services on 6257 4377 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

If you have been affected by sexual violence, or someone you know has, you can report it to police by attending a police station or phoning 131 444.

australia.title: Coalition divided over tougher gambling laws – with MPs warning Angus Taylor against overreach
australia.snippet: Some Liberal and National MPs warn against overregulation in party-room discussion, while others argue for more stringent rules Follow ou...
australia.content:
Coalition MPs have warned the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, not to overreach in talks with Anthony Albanese on Labor’s gambling advertising crackdown, insisting rules that are too stringent would not strike the right balance on personal responsibility.

The prime minister and the opposition leader met several times on Tuesday to negotiate on Labor’s legislation on gambling, with restrictions on betting inducements, paring back TV advertising hours and tweaking rules for streaming platforms among possible avenues for reform after Albanese signalled a willingness to amend his own bill.

While a clutch of newer MPs, including the outspoken advocate Simon Kennedy, have called for the Coalition to seek more amendments, it is understood more senior members of the party room are less inclined to push for sweeping changes, with Taylor expected to agree to a few more modest tweaks. A deal on amendments could be agreed in time for the bill to be debated in parliament on Wednesday.

Debate over gambling dominated a meeting of the joint Coalition party room in Canberra on Tuesday, with nine Liberal and Nationals MPs making their views known to colleagues.

Among the contributions were five MPs pushing for tougher restrictions and four arguing the Coalition needed “to get the balance right” and not go too far in limiting ads. Some warned overly restrictive rules for Australian gambling companies could push some punters to illegal overseas operators, citing comparisons with the rise of illegal tobacco amid rising government excise pushing up retail prices.

Taylor himself raised the question of personal responsibility in a media conference on Monday, an issue that was also raised in Tuesday’s meeting alongside concerns about “overregulation”.

Coalition MPs used the meeting to raise concerns about “perceived behaviour of gambling preying on the vulnerable”, but the possibility of a deal remained “a moving feast” as parliament resumed after the winter break.

The gambling industry is increasingly resigned to the paring back of inducements, but it says that such restrictions could send gamblers to unregulated offshore operators and particularly impinge the earnings of smaller wagering operators.

Industry sources said they were seeking to warn Coalition MPs about the impact of further changes to inducements or ad rules, but rejected claims from the Greens that they were intimately involved in negotiations.

While Labor sources say they are still confident Taylor will get on board, the Greens are also still talking with the government, signalling a deal with the Coalition is not yet done. Albanese on Monday said publicly he would “later this week” have progress on inducements and advertising rules.

Labor has been criticised for falling short of the ambition of a parliamentary inquiry led by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy three years ago, and is talking with the Coalition and the Greens to find a pathway through the Senate. Murphy’s 2023 committee recommended the government “prohibit all online gambling inducements and inducement advertising, and that it do so without delay”.

Guardian Australia understands some small tweaks to the timing of TV advertising, specifically to lessen the impact on children, were among issues being considered in Labor’s negotiations with the Coalition and Greens.

Labor’s proposed changes would see gambling ads restricted to three an hour on broadcast TV between 6am and 8.30pm, but further timing tweaks were part of discussions.

Other changes potentially up for discussion include what was described as a “discrepancy” in ad rules for broadcast TV as opposed to streaming services. Online platforms, under Labor’s proposal, are not subject to the timing rules of broadcast TV, and would instead require a “triple lock” – users have to be logged-in, age verified and provided an opt-out option – to be able to show gambling ads.

A change to an opt-in provision, rather than opt-out, for streaming ads is also being discussed, but was not expected to be among the final amendments agreed with Taylor.

Kennedy, one of the Liberal MPs pushing for tougher action, used a speech in parliament to call for an independent review of the rules after the next election. That plan would help make any newly introduced protections even stronger within three years.

Kennedy said there were “two glaring gaps” in the existing laws: inducements to keep punters gambling longer and unlimited advertising online.

“There should be an independent review of wherever we land after the next election, so we can do more,” Kennedy said.

The government is expected to make amendments to the bill in the lower house, where the bill is listed for debate on Wednesday.

australia.title: Delivery drivers to be paid minimum $31.30 an hour across Australia in ‘world-leading’ decision
australia.snippet: Fair Work Commission issues a new minimum standards order for gig workers to come into effect 17 August Get our breaking news email , fre...
australia.content:
Delivery drivers in Australia will be paid a minimum rate of $31.30 (US $22.05/£16.35) an hour and insured for injuries on the job under a landmark agreement approved by the industrial umpire that could set a precedent in other countries.

The Fair Work Commission (FWC) on Tuesday issued a new minimum standards order for gig workers who perform on-demand delivery of food, drinks, or groceries, and the operators of the digital platforms who engage their services.

The Transport Workers’ Union, representing the gig workers, had jointly applied with major platforms DoorDash and UberEats for the new protections in 2024, after years of talks.

After taking public submissions on new standards for the industry, including from gig workers and other interested parties including Amazon and Auspost, FWC has greenlit the conditions, to come into effect from 17 August.

The deal is likely to have involved concessions from either side of the negotiating table, including the union agreeing to call the workers “employee-like”.

In a joint statement on Tuesday, the TWU, UberEats and DoorDash said the new standards would provide an “industry-wide safety net for hundreds of thousands of [workers] while preserving the flexibility that sits at the heart of on-demand work.”

The TWU national secretary Michael Kaine said the new standards were “world-leading”.

Under the new standards, workers will be responsible for maintaining third-party insurances on the vehicles they use for deliveries, so if they get in an accident and damage another vehicle the delivery platform will not be liable for the cost.

On the other hand, delivery platforms will have to organise and pay for personal accident insurance that “provides a reasonable minimum level of cover” for their workers, although experts have previously pointed out this is open to interpretation.

While they were proposed by the TWU, UberEats and DoorDash, the conditions are expected to apply to any on-demand platforms that sell food, drinks or groceries, as well as the people they hire on an ad hoc basis to deliver products.

The new conditions include “safety net” pay rates for workers, who will initially receive hourly rates ranging from $31.30 to $32 depending on the class of vehicle – for example, whether they are riding a push bike or driving a car.

The minimum rates – which are designed to ensure delivery workers are paid even if they are, for example, waiting for a restaurant – will increase by 50 cents from 1 January 2027.

The new standards cover a range of issues and, among other provisions, are intended to provide clearer dispute resolution and workers the right to unpaid time off.

The TWU, DoorDash and UberEats made the joint application to the FWC after the Albanese government introduced workplace reforms in 2023, which included empowering the industrial umpire to set minimum standards for gig workers.

The workplace relations minister, Amanda Rishworth, on Tuesday said the resulting standards were a “milestone”.

“This [FWC] order is a big step in delivering Australia’s world-leading gig worker protections and means food delivery workers don’t have to trade off flexibility for fairer protections,” she said.

australia.title: Lobbyist defends ‘shit sheet’ on former Liberal MP despite admitting he knew ‘there was no affair’, Icac hears
australia.snippet: Consultant Jeremy Greenwood gives evidence to Independent Commission Against Corruption as it investigates allegations linked to Christia...
australia.content:
A lobbyist under investigation by the New South Wales corruption watchdog has admitted to commissioning a “shit sheet” on a former Liberal MP, knowing a reference to a purported extramarital affair was untrue, an inquiry has heard.

The consultant and lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood gave his second day of evidence to the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s (Icac) Operation Rosny on Tuesday.

Greenwood is named in two of the watchdog’s allegations. He is among three Liberal figures who allegedly took donations from Jean Nassif, a fugitive property developer, in exchange for the pursuit of outcomes including damage to the career of the former NSW Liberal minister and MP David Elliott.

On Tuesday, Greenwood was asked about a document titled “David Elliott shit sheet.docx”, which he emailed to himself in December 2020.

The inquiry previously heard from Dylan Whitelaw, a former employee of ChristianEllis and Greenwood at registered lobbying company Beckington, that he had been asked by Greenwood to write part of the document.

Greenwood accepted this evidence, but like Whitelaw told the commission he did not write a section with the sub-heading “extramarital affair”.

Following Whitelaw’s evidence, during which he accepted under cross-examination that no such affair had taken place, Elliott issued a statement rejecting the allegations. Greenwood admitted that when he sent the document to himself, with a view to using it to discredit Elliott, he knew the affair to be untrue.

“To make it very clear, particularly for Mr Elliott’s family, we figured out pretty quickly there was no affair,” he said.

But Greenwood rejected that the document, which he said was never circulated, had been created to benefit Nassif, saying “there was an ongoing thing with [Elliott] from well before I met Jean Nassif”.

“David Elliott was actively attacking Beckington, Christian, and myself, and I think it’s perfectly fine to have defence on this,” he said. Elliott has been contacted for comment.

‘Jessica’ the fake administrative assistant

On Tuesday, the inquiry heard that Beckington, which allegedly accepted illegal donations to fund factional Liberal party work, created a fake administrative assistant called “Jessica”.

Icac is investigating whether the company was used by a Christian Liberal factional group known as the Reformers to solicit or accept prohibited donations for the recruitment or renewal of members to the party. The practice, known as branch stacking, is not itself illegal.

The group wanted more conservative policies on issues such as same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia.

Icac has heard that Beckington, set up by Greenwood and Ellis in 2019, accepted payments for factional work through fake invoices to Michael O’Hara, a prohibited donor, and the schools governing body Catholic Schools NSW. Greenwood has said he cannot recall either arrangement.

On Tuesday, counsel assisting, Peggy Dwyer SC, read out 2020 correspondence from Beckington to Catholic Schools NSW with invoices, signed “Kind regards, Jessica”. “Who’s Jessica?” she asked.

“Sorry, I’m not laughing,” said Greenwood. “Jessica was a fake admin name Christian created. He just thought it was funny.”

After Dwyer said she was “not getting the joke”, Greenwood said: “We have silly humour. Sorry.”

Greenwood repeatedly said he could not recall if the company paid Reformers members to do factional work. He said he believed the company had made payments to Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of the former premier Dominic Perrottet. Dominic Perrottet is not named in Icac’s allegations.

“If he wanted money, we looked after him,” said Greenwood, who later admitted to a payment of $12,000 to Jean-Claude Perrottet, who he described as his “favourite friend”.

Ellis moved to the UK at the start of this year, and the inquiry has heard he declined to give oral evidence, but on Monday Greenwood insisted his friend did want to give evidence.

On Tuesday, the inquiry heard Ellis rang Greenwood at 6am on encrypted messaging app Signal.

Greenwood said Ellis had asked him: “‘What was the reaction to you saying I wanted to appear?’ And I said, ‘Just noted.’” He said he could not recall if he had discussed payments to Jean-Claude Perrottet with Ellis.

Greenwood, who is named in two of the watchdog’s allegations, has repeatedly disputed being a member of the Reformers.

He was asked about being privy to and responding to messages in which the Reformers discussed recruitment work. Greenwood repeatedly said he was not an “active participant” in group chats.

Greenwood will give evidence to the commission again on Wednesday, the watchdog confirmed. The witness on Thursday and Friday will be the Catholic Schools CEO, Dallas McInerney.

On Tuesday, Dwyer read out a 2021 text exchange from Greenwood to McInerney claiming that the Nationals senator Matt Canavan, Greenwood’s former boss, had asked McInerney to pass on a message to the moderate Liberal Dave Sharma.

Canavan was purportedly concerned about Sharma’s plan to remove a section of the Religious Discrimination Act, which allows religious schools to discriminate against students on the basis of their sexuality in certain circumstances. McInerney said he had texted Sharma and the Liberal moderate Andrew Bragg for “urgent conversations”.

Canavan, Sharma and Bragg are not accused of any wrongdoing.

Icac’s inquiry continues.
