    Good morning

What we learned today, Tuesday 11 August

It’s been a jam-packed day as parliament returned for its first sitting fortnight after the winter break.

Before we wrap up our live coverage for the day, let’s take a look at the top headlines:

  • The Reserve Bank held the cash rate at 4.35% in a widely expected decision despite persistent worries about elevated inflation.

  • Anthony Albanese is facing criticism after appearing to joke on a podcast about a gift of melons from the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, which he has refused to apologise for.

  • Kate Chaney, who was on the inquiry with the late Labor MP Peta Murphy that handed down the landmark gambling harm report You win some, you lose more, says so far it seems the talks between the Coalition and Labor on a gambling reform package are “disappointing”.

  • The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has announced delays to the government’s nation-first bill to legislate a right to work from home two days a week, adding it won’t take effect until after the election.

  • The federal agriculture minister, Julie Collins, says priority species of birds in captivity will be the first to be vaccinated against H5 bird flu, with the rollout to begin soon.

  • Liberal and Nationals MPs had their weekly catchup at Parliament House, with the meeting including interesting discussions about the government’s plans to limit online gambling advertising.

  • Two more KPMG bosses have stepped down ahead of a parliamentary grilling over the firm’s audit leaks scandal, which has now prompted nine high-profile resignations.

  • The Fair Work Ombudsman has announced it will investigate an increasingly popular Australian gig-work app for the hospitality industry after concerns were raised about workers missing out on entitlements.

  • Parliament sat for its first question time since returning from the winter break. Here’s a tl;dr on what happened.

Thanks for joining us, see you tomorrow!

Parliamentary committee backs White Australia’s listing as a prohibited hate group

The Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security (PJCIS) has backed the federal government’s decision to list White Australia as a prohibited hate group in May.

The committee was established to conduct an independent review of the listing and has found that White Australia met the criteria for the designation under the new laws passed earlier this year.

The committee found White Australia “has engaged in conduct constituting hate crimes and that the listing is necessary to protect Australians from harm”.

The PJCIS chair, Senator Raff Ciccone, said:

For too long, organisations like White Australia have been able to spread hate and create a pathway for others to engage in violence.

Australia will not tolerate groups that promote hatred, normalise extremist rhetoric and put the safety of Australians at risk.

Benita Kolovos

Georgie Purcell likely to lose her seat in Victoria’s voting changes

The Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell will also likely lose her seat in changes to Victoria’s group voting tickets.

She says parties that used GVTs were “simply operating under the system that was granted to us to get elected”.

She says it’s been particularly “galling” to hear allegations during the debate that the crossbench MPs elected under GVTs had done “deals” with the government. Purcell says:

I mean, I’m standing here today at the end of the term with duck shooting, jumps racing, greyhound racing still [legal] here in Victoria. It’s because we have chosen to be collaborative and proactive members of parliament and take our jobs representing our communities really, really seriously. So some of the commentary that has come up in this debate has been pretty disappointing. To be completely honest, we are all still your colleagues. We all still have to spend time together until the end of this term.

She also criticised the government for ramming the legislation through both houses of parliament just weeks before the election. She said the Animal Justice party had asked the government for eight years to pair the abolition of group voting ticket with other changes in the upper house, such as scrapping the eight regions and moving to a single statewide electorate. But this would require a referendum.

Cait Kelly

Border force raids more than 100 service stations in crackdown on illegal tobacco and vapes

More than 100 Metro Petroleum service stations have been raided as part of a major investigation into the distribution of illegal tobacco and vapes.

About 250 law enforcement and regulatory officers from 15 agencies targeted the stations across Queensland, New South Wales, the Australian Capital Territory, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia.

In a statement, the Australian Border Force said:

Operation SHORTHAND was established following an intelligence referral into the NDG [National Disruption Group] by the Australian Federal Police and the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, identifying alleged links between the service stations, suspected criminal activity and the alleged sale of illicit tobacco and vapes.

The operation remains active, with the NDG and partner agencies continuing to assess materials and information gathered during enforcement activities.

Further details, including official outcomes from the operation, will be announced in due course.

Metro has been contacted for comment. The owners are not accused of any wrongdoing.

Benita Kolovos

Group voting tickets debate in Victoria continues

Several crossbench MPs are expected to lose their seats as a result of the changes. They include the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers MP, Jeff Bourman, who said the reforms are only happening now because the major parties expect to lose seats at the November state election. Or as he put it:

No one really cared because it worked for them. Now, it doesn’t work for them. Now we have basically something I feel has been put up by a bunch of bedwetters that sleep with the lights on at night. I think this is really, really what’s going on. There was panic stations. Chicken Little, the sky’s falling in. Well, you reap what you sow, fellas and ladies. Come the next election, I feel that election is going to be studied for decades because of the disaster for the major parties.

Bourman said he expected One Nation would be “the largest party” in the upper house, thanks in part to this change and for MPs to “enjoy what’s left” of the chamber.

The preference whisperer Glenn Druery has also made a similar argument against GVTs, claiming One Nation could win between 13 and 16 upper house seats as a result.

Benita Kolovos

Group voting ticket debate under way in Victoria’s upper house

As we mentioned earlier, the Victorian parliament’s upper house is now debating a bill that will scrap group voting tickets (GVTs) – a system of voting ripe for preference harvesting.

Under GVTs, voters can only choose one party above the line on the ballot paper, with their preferences then allocated by the party if it’s knocked out during counting. It has allowed backroom deals between parties to flourish, enabling some candidates to get elected with only a minuscule number of primary votes.

The electoral amendment (miscellaneous matters) bill 2026, if passed, will replace GVTs with a new above-the-line voting system that requires voters to number at least five groups in order of preference. Those preferences will then flow to candidates in the order they appear below the line for each party or group.

The Labor MP Ryan Batchelor says the reform is “long overdue” and will bring the state in line with every other similar jurisdiction:

It will place decisions about voter preferences in the hands of voters, and there can be nothing that is more fundamentally democratic than that. This is a reform that has been recommended by the Electoral Matters Committee, a joint committee of this parliament, on several occasions, including most recently in two reports in the last couple of years.

The Coalition will support the bill, with the Liberal MP David Davis saying Labor has been “very tardy” in bringing on the reform. He claimed that when the Liberals were last in government in 2014 they approached the then opposition leader Daniel Andrews to reform the system but he refused:

There was a discussion there, and we would have supported it at that point in time. But let’s also be clear: there is every reason to be supportive of this [now] because there have been some terrible, undemocratic outcomes that have been engineered through the group voting ticket.

Benita Kolovos

Following on our earlier post, the Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson, has criticised the government’s reforms to “close every loophole” used by high-profile accused and convicted criminals to hide their identities in court.

She says when she first became leader in late 2025, her first priority was to introduce a standalone coercive control offence:

Victoria could have already had standalone coercive control, if Labor had supported our legislation. Instead, Labor played politics with women’s safety, only to introduce its own laws five minutes to midnight. Coercive control is an insidious form of abuse and can affect anyone, but we know women are overwhelmingly the victims of intimate partner violence. Protecting women and victim-survivors from abuse should never be political. We will always stand on the side of victim-survivors.

Here’s what we wrote at the time:

Josh Butler

Allow voluntary assisted dying debate, crossbenchers urge Labor

Members of the crossbench are pleading with Labor to take action on allowing voluntary assisted dying consultatons via telehealth, with the advocate and former TV favourite Andrew Denton saying people in the last stages of their life should have more options.

The independent MP Kate Chaney tried to bring on a debate on the issue in the lower house today, but the Labor government waved off the attempt. The Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young said she would try to bring on debate about a similar bill in the Senate.

The debate is about whether to allow VAD via telehealth, which is now banned. Advocates say this means people with terminal illnesses have to appear in-person at a doctor, which presents particular problems for people in rural or remote areas. Denton, the former TV interviewer, told a press conference today about the case of a man in Melbourne with advanced motor neurone disease, whose condition made it that he soiled himself as his wife drove him to visit his doctor for a euthanasia assessment.

Labor’s national conference resolved that the government should change the law, but so far no debate has been allowed.

Chaney said it would be a “simple fix”, with all states and territories allowing VAD except the Northern Territory, which will legalise the practice this month. She said no safeguards would need to be altered to allow VAD consultations via telehealth. She was supported by fellow independent Monique Ryan, who said “every day that we fail to pass this legislation is a day that Australians continue to suffer unnecessarily, and the people who care for them are unable to provide them with the support that they need and they deserve”.

Denton called on parliament to resolve the issue as soon as possible. He said:

A government and a parliament’s first responsibility is to protect its citizens. Right now, this government and this parliament are failing to do that.

Benita Kolovos

Long-called-for reforms introduced to Victorian parliament

At the Victorian parliament today, much attention focused on the Labor government’s election commitment to “close every loophole” used by high-profile accused and convicted criminals to hide their identities in court. But the government also introduced a bill to parliament that includes other reforms long called for by victim-survivors of sexual violence.

The attorney general, Sonya Kilkenny, outlined several of the reforms when she first read the bill into the house a few hours ago. They include:

  • Criminalising coercive control as a standalone offence.

  • Abolishing good character as a mitigating factor in sentencing.

  • Making it unlawful to discriminate against someone because they have experienced or are experiencing family violence.

  • Expanding the jurisdiction of a criminal court to extend or vary a family violence intervention order so victims do not have to keep telling their story and reliving their trauma.

  • Requiring the court to consider the views and safety of a victim-survivor when extending a family violence intervention order.

  • Expanding the personal safety intervention order framework to recognise grooming as a prohibited behaviour.

  • Expanding relief and exemptions under Victoria’s fines system for victim-survivors to stop the financial impact of perpetrators using the system to abuse their partner.

The Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell says she first urged the government to introduce the family violence protection in March. She says the reform will save lives:

Until now, a loophole in our anti-discrimination laws has resulted in Victorian women being legally sacked by their employer for disclosing their experiences of family violence. This change isn’t just symbolic – and it won’t just ensure protection from discrimination in workplaces. It will extend to all areas of a victim-survivor’s life – including housing, healthcare and banking. This is a meaningful reform that will save lives by helping victims safely leave abusive relationships without losing income or becoming homeless.

Greens accuse Carroll of ‘crumbling to big business’ on work from home

Benita Kolovos

The Victorian Greens have accused the new premier, Ben Carroll, of “crumbling to big business” after he announced this morning the government would delay debate on work from home laws and push back its commencement until 1 July 2027.

The Greens say the delay will particularly hurt women, carers and disabled people who stand to benefit most from flexible work, as they will now have to wait another 10 months for rights they fought for and were promised.

The party’s state leader, Ellen Sandell, says:

The new premier has barely moved into his new office and he’s already crumbling to big business and their tantrums. Workers were weeks away from finally getting these hard-earned rights. Then the corporate lobby came knocking and the new Labor premier rolled over. Women, carers and disabled people might now be forced back into commuting full-time for at least another 10 months because the new premier has decided keeping big business happy matters more than making working people’s lives easier.

More here:

Tom McIlroy

‘No excuses’ on Murphy report recommendations, Anglican archbishop says

Sydney’s Anglican archbishop, Kanishka Raffel, has urged federal parliament to implement the full recommendations of the Murphy review on online gambling advertising.

Amid negotiations between Labor and the Coalition this week, Raffel said the late Labor MP Peta Murphy was right to recommend a full, phased-in ban on gambling advertising and inducements from betting companies.

The Murphy recommendations give a sensible and balance blueprint for gambling regulation.

They protect our children and families.

They must be implemented in full – there are no excuses for not doing so.

Anglican Churches from around Australia have been meeting in Melbourne and without dissent, we have agreed that the Murphy report should be adopted in full for “the welfare and public health of our nation’s young people and other vulnerable persons”.

RBA warns further rises possible in fight against inflation

The Reserve Bank of Australia governor, Michele Bullock, has warned further interest rate rises remain possible as the bank continues to monitor inflationary pressures.

Speaking in Sydney after the RBA’s decision to leave the cash rate unchanged at 4.35%, Bullock said the board had not considered a cut at its meeting.

The board did not discuss an interest rate cut at this meeting. It only discussed a raise/stay.

The main game here for us is excess capacity, tight labour market, particularly in some areas like construction, the Middle East conflict, the AI boom; these are all the things that are front of mind in terms of risks to the inflation outlook.

Bullock acknowledged that “this is a difficult period for some households” but said the board was “not ruling out” further increases.

The board will be closely watching for evidence of upside risks to inflation materialising. High inflation hurts all Australians, especially the most vulnerable, and that’s why inflation, bringing inflation down, is our priority.

The board isn’t ruling out there may be a need for further interest rate rises if we look like we’re off a path that takes us with inflation remaining above the target for much longer in the forecasts.

We’re saying we want to get a bit more information to confirm whether or not we still seem to be on that path.

Krishani Dhanji

Thank you all for following along on the blog with me today, I’ll leave you with the brilliant Achol Arok.

Stay tuned for the Reserve Bank governor shortly, and I’ll see you back here bright and early tomorrow!

Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time

  • The opposition pushed Labor on the cost of living, and tried to get the prime minister to apologise over melon-gate.

  • On the former, the opposition targeted Labor over the so-called “widow tax” and claimed the negative gearing and capital gains tax changes had “tanked” the housing market.

  • On the latter, Anthony Albanese twice refused to apologise to prime minister Sanae Takaichi.

  • The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, was kicked out.

  • Albanese completely avoided a question by the Greens on whether the government would implement a gas export tax – refusing to even say the words gas or tax in his answer.

After a final dixer to Amanda Rishworth, the PM calls time on QT for today.

Should coal and gas companies be forced to put money aside to fund cleanups?

When will the government force coal and gas companies to put money aside to fully fund the cleanup of their projects, asks the independent MP Allegra Spender.

She says that renters have to pay a bond and a cleanup fee before moving into a home, but fossil fuel companies aren’t expected to do the same, which can leave the commonwealth footing a cleanup bill – citing a recent case where a gas producer went into administration.

The resources minister, Madeleine King, says that in the case Spender has raised, there will be no taxpayer money going to any cleanup.

I want to make it really clear again that taxpayers will not be left to foot the bill if companies do not do the right thing in respect of this particular project. I want to make clear insolvency does not excuse title holders from decommissioning responsibilities, and the government is considering all enforcement options to hold responsible title holders and related parties accountable.

Kevin Hogan comes with a multiple choice question

The Nationals frontbencher Kevin Hogan comes to QT with a multiple choice question today – how fun. He asks whether rents have reportedly increased by 10% since the 2026 budget because of:

A. Record high immigration outpacing new home builds.

B. Labor’s toxic taxes on housing.

C. The 15 interest rate rises under Labor.

Or D. All of the above.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, takes the question and says the housing market has been influenced by a number of factors, and that the market was already cooling before the budget was handed down.

Chalmers basically says that the issues are not the sole fault of the budget, and that the volatility in the housing market and immigration numbers were there before May.

We have had for some time now upward pressure on rents, partly because of a decade of neglect, we haven’t had enough homes in our community, Mr Speaker, and we are taking the necessary steps to build more homes.

When it comes to migration, I understand that those opposite want to go about this in the most divisive way that they can, but they need to recognise that net overseas migration has come down 45% since its peak.

Albanese avoids question on gas export tax

Back to the crossbench, the Greens MP Elizabeth Watson-Brown asks the PM if he’ll listen to the public “instead of the gas lobby and implement a minimum 25% tax on gas exports?” She also notes that at the most recent Labor national conference, ordinary party members and MPs pushed to hold a vote for a gas export tax.

Anthony Albanese doesn’t say the words gas or tax (let alone together) in his answer.

Instead he takes aim at the Greens, saying he’s somewhat surprised at getting a question from the party that hold “secret conferences”.

What we do, in stark contrast, is have a conference that is broadcast live on national TV for all to see. We have the election of 400 delegates and 400 proxy delegates who represent workers, who represent local branch members, who represent regions right around Australia.

PM probed on skyrocketing mortgages; Tim Wilson gets yeeted

Angus Taylor stays on the economy, and asks the prime minister to confirm the average new mortgage holder is paying $29,000 a year more in interest alone since Labor came into power – after 15 interest rate rises.

Anthony Albanese says he understands households are doing it tough, and then rolls through a list of cost-of-living measures the government has undertaken.

Every day we look at doing something about it – not just identifying grievance, but producing solutions, not protesting.

Albanese isn’t answering the actual question, so Dan Tehan gets up to make a point of order.

Milton Dick agrees with Tehan and tells Albanese to stay focused, and the PM continues:

Someone in this place said on the 10th November 2020, nobody wins from low interest rates … Going back, in case you think that was an accident, in 2018, we need to create the policy settings to progressively increase interest rates. Money is too cheap, and it’s time we did something about it around the policy framework. The question for this leader of the opposition: Why did he make this man the shadow treasurer?

Tim Wilson, not too happy about being quoted here, yells out to the PM in response, which gets him kicked out by Dick for the rest of QT.

australia.title: RBA interest rates: Reserve Bank holds cash rate at 4.35% but threatens more hikes if needed
australia.snippet: In a widely expected decision, the Reserve Bank of Australia holds interest rate after three hikes earlier this year Follow our Australia...
australia.content:
The Reserve Bank of Australia has held the official cash rate at 4.35% but warned higher interest rates are “quite possible” even if house prices keep falling.

Tuesday’s decision to hold was predicted by economists and financial markets, after three rate rises this year hit property values across the capital cities.

The RBA board unanimously voted to leave rates on pause, saying in a statement “the economy appears to be slowing as expected”.

The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, told reporters after the announcement that the board had considered raising rates, with each board member worried inflation was still too high.

“It’s important people believe that we will act if we need to,” Bullock said.

“I think personally that it’s quite possible we might need to go but we’ll wait and see what the data tells us.”

Markets raised their bets on another hike in Australia by the year’s end, from 53% before the decision to 69% on Tuesday afternoon. Shane Oliver, chief economist at AMP, said traders had responded to Bullock’s strong warnings.

The bank’s updated forecasts on Tuesday showed inflation was lower than expected this year as fuel prices had fallen but would not return towards the targeted 2.5% until early 2028, even if rates edged upwards.

Bullock said the board believed that was a “reasonable” timeline to bring inflation back to the low target level.

The bank has forecast stronger jobs growth but higher unemployment than it expected in May, reaching 4.7% by the end of 2027.

Stephen Smith, a partner at Deloitte Access Economics, said the forecasts suggested the RBA “increasingly feels its job may be done”.

“However, another rate rise in 2026 cannot be fully ruled out,” he said.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said Tuesday’s decision to hold was “welcome” amid uncertainty in the global economy.

“This will come as a relief to Australians with a mortgage,” Chalmers said.

Housing not ‘the main game’

The RBA on Tuesday said the housing market had slowed more than expected in the wake of rate rises and the federal budget.

New home loans have already begun to slow. Investor loan commitments in June had fallen by roughly a quarter compared with the start of the year, as a share of total housing credit, the RBA reported.

The bank warned falling house prices would weigh on household spending and per person economic activity, as consumers who owned property felt poorer.

ANZ economists on Tuesday released separate forecasts predicting capital cities’ home prices would fall at least 5%, with Sydney to fall 14.5%.

Bullock said the housing downturn was not “the main game” in Tuesday’s decision, with the RBA instead watching for strong jobs creation, tight capacity in the economy, the AI boom and the effects of the Middle East conflict.

“The housing market wasn’t a constraint,” Bullock said. “That’s not entering the equation.”

She noted housing prices had risen by about 50% since 2020.

Less than 1% of homeowners were in negative equity and the RBA believed even a 20% fall in house prices would mean about 5% of people were in negative equity, Bullock said.

The RBA’s updated statement on monetary policy said mortgage holders have kept ahead on repayments as rates rise, with seven in eight borrowers holding almost a year or more worth of repayments in their offset and redraw accounts.

The RBA predicted a recovery in house prices, along with falling interest rates, could push per person economic activity back up again by 2028.

“We still have a shortage of supply … that is going to resolve somehow in prices,” Bullock said.

The RBA also upgraded its predictions for business investment as demand for datacentre construction grows. Its statement said businesses had reported no issues finding workers and materials for datacentre projects.

But Bullock warned the projects could add to inflation as there was evidence they were taking construction workers away from the housing sector.

“There’s already an area, which is under pressure, and it’s under more pressure because of datacentre investment in Australia,” she said.

“If it puts a lot of pressure on some of these areas that are very tight, then it is possible that it keeps inflation elevated before we get the productivity improvements that we’re hoping for.”

world.title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy
world.snippet: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta Spain has announced it will introduce tempora...
world.content:
Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.

The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.

Hours earlier, Spain threatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.

The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.

The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.

The Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.

Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.

“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.

He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.

Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.

Meloni’s office said in a statement: “Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control.

“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered.”

Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures within hours.

Spanish police have been monitoring online rumours and social media about possible fresh arrivals in Ceuta in mid-August, according to local media. But authorities have not expressly said they expect a repeat of last week’s rush.

Border authorities would in the meantime “do their utmost to ensure maximum ease of movement for Spanish and European citizens” who are not affected by border checks, the Italian statement added.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, introduced border controls at maritime and air entry points for third-country nationals arriving from Spain.

The move, announced on 31 July, was an “extraordinary measure” intended to “safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation”, Meloni said at the time.

She was among several EU leaders who called for Spain to be suspended from the visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Ceuta incident, despite such a move being legally impossible.

Italy’s coalition government has sought to stop the tens of thousands of people who land in small boats on the country’s shores each year.

The Spanish government warned against “creating rifts and sterile conflicts driven by internal electoral motives” and said “we trust that pro-European sentiment, common sense and good faith prevail”.

Of the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta, 70,000 have returned to Morocco, according to official Spanish figures.

Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossings.

Moroccan rights groups, however, estimate the figure to be higher. The Moroccan Association for Human Rights and the European Coordination for Human Rights in Morocco on Friday said at least 141 deaths were recorded and that the toll was likely to rise.

Morocco’s interior ministry has said 11 people died on its side of the border, all but one by drowning.

Those who remain in Ceuta – including hundreds of unaccompanied children – face dire living conditions with little access to food, water and shelter.

world.title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections
world.snippet: Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians Temporary protected status...
world.content:
Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.

On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.

Saris’s decision follows a 6-3 supreme court ruling in June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US.

The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians.

A TPS designation allows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally.

In her 15-page ruling, Saris wrote that “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”.

According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially.

“South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote.

In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counsel said on X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same! Every day these ‘administrative stays’ are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.”

The Guardian has contacted African Communities Together for comment.

Meanwhile, in a statement on Friday, the immigrant advocacy organization Global Refuge condemned the ruling. The CEO, Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, said: “The reality of the situation is that South Sudan is on the brink of a return to an all-out-civil war. Roughly two-thirds of the population, some 10 million people, now depend on humanitarian aid to survive.

“With only several hundred South Sudanese holding TPS in the US right now, this isn’t a policy forced by scale or strain on our system. To the contrary, this is the administration’s deliberate choice to send a small group of vulnerable individuals and families back into a country where civilians are bearing the brunt of intensifying violence and displacement,” Vignarajah added.

The Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants comes despite the US government’s own highest-level travel warnings for Americans to several countries affected, including South Sudan, Haiti and Syria.

In the case of South Sudan, the country has been ravaged by years of civil war and political instability that have displaced millions. Since gaining independence in 2011, more than 400,000 people have been killed in conflict, with fighting and ethnic violence continuing to claim civilian lives.

The DHS moved in November to terminate TPS for South Sudan, saying the country ‌no longer met the conditions for the designation, which was first issued in 2011. The department’s action would have led to the end of protections for more than 232 South Sudanese and at least 73 South Sudanese with pending applications. An earlier order by Saris had blocked that from happening.

After the supreme court’s ruling, lawyers for a group of South Sudanese nationals and the non-profit African Communities Together urged Saris to once again block the ‌end of TPS on new grounds that the justices had not addressed.

That included an argument that the DHS lacked authority to terminate TPS because the statute that created the TPS program in 1990 referred ​only to the attorney general as the official who had authority to extend and terminate the deportation protections.

The DHS was established later, in 2002, after the September 11 attacks.

Most of the justice department’s immigration-related functions were transferred to it at that time. Saris, who was appointed by Bill Clinton, concluded Congress had likewise transferred authority over TPS to the DHS.

Since 2001, TPS holders have paid $7.8bn annually in taxes and contributed $262bn to the US economy, according to the advocacy organization Fwd.us. Many TPS holders are employed in critical industries already facing worker shortages across the country, including construction, hospitality and healthcare.

Losing TPS can leave immigrants without legal status vulnerable to arrest, detention and deportation, even with pending asylum or green card applications.

Some may face immigration court proceedings with limited options to stay in the US. People ordered removed could be deported and barred from returning for years.

Reuters contributed reporting

world.title: Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say
world.snippet: Cases have passed 4,000 and health watchdog plans to go door to door to find patients in major response escalation The virus causing a ma...
world.content:
The virus causing a massive outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo could be mutating, health officials fear, as confirmed cases pass 4,000.

Africa’s public health watchdog said the time for incremental action was over as they announced plans to scale up every aspect of the response and go “door to door” looking for patients.

The Ebola outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first reported on 15 May, although there are suspicions the disease could have been spreading since January.

There have been 3,973 cases and 1,801 deaths recorded as of 4 August, according to the DRC’s national public health institute. Speaking on Thursday, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), told a press briefing cases had topped 4,000.

The outbreak is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. There are eight times more cases, and six times more deaths than were recorded 11 weeks into the West Africa Ebola outbreak in 2014-18, which infected more than 28,000 people and killed at least 11,000.

Kaseya said he had spoken to the director general of the World Health Organization, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, and they planned studies “to check if there is no additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating. Because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented.”

More than two-thirds of Ebola deaths are happening in the community rather than in treatment centres. In a treatment centre run by MSF in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province, 90% of admitted patients do not appear on authorities’ lists of contacts of known cases. Both factors indicate high levels of untracked transmission.

Kaseya said contact tracing in the DRC was insufficient, with only 10 contacts identified for every Ebola patient, when about 40 would be the expected number.

Ebola is a viral haemorrhagic fever that can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, organ damage and internal bleeding. The outbreak is centred on the conflict-affected mining province of Ituri, but has spread to Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo. There were 20 cases recorded in neighbouring Uganda before it brought its outbreak under control.

Dr Wessam Mankoula, acting head of emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC, said response teams planned a shift “from contact tracing to active case search”, which would mean community health workers “moving from door to door” asking households if they had anyone sick with Ebola symptoms.

He added: “I think the time for incremental action is over and we’re starting now the phase for scaling up.”

Kaseya promised a “village-centered response” that would involve communities, more use of digital tools and greater action in the camps for people who have been internally displaced by conflict in affected provinces.

Officials also said they planned to begin using antiviral remdesivir on a compassionate use basis to treat patients. They will also start testing whether Ervebo, a vaccine licensed for use against a different strain of Ebola, should be offered in the affected province, after receiving data suggesting that Bundibugyo caused less serious disease and “zero death” among people who had received that jab.

“Seeing the expansion of this outbreak, only the public health measure will not be enough to quickly control or stop this outbreak,” said Dr Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC director of research, clinical trials and innovation.

DRC authorities said they were investigating a suspected Ebola death on a boat heading to the capital, Kinshasa, from the north-east of the country, and that the other passengers on board would be quarantined and tested.

Unicef warned that essential healthcare was being disrupted by the outbreak as fear of infection and service disruptions kept families away from clinics. In the outbreak’s centre, the mining town of Mongbwalu, the proportion of children receiving their first measles dose has fallen 69%.

world.title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
world.snippet: State department informs Congress of planned closures in Canada, Grenada, Japan, Indonesia and Cameroon The US state department is to shu...
world.content:
The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China.

The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada.

The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants.

More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association.

Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China.

“China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee.

“The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?”

The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods.

Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital.

Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests.

“I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto.

“It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.”

A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.”

China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”.

A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time.

“We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.”

In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China.

“Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said.

The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions.

Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

world.title: Top Ugandan footballer killed by robbers armed with paving stones
world.snippet: David Owori, who played for the national team, died in hospital after he tried to stop robbers taking his phone The Ugandan football comm...
world.content:
The Ugandan football community is in mourning after the death of a player who was fatally injured during a robbery in the capital, Kampala, on Tuesday night.

David Owori, who captained Sports Club Villa, a Uganda Premier League club, and represented the national team, was attacked after resisting an attempt to steal his mobile phone and other belongings near his home in Makindye division.

Racheal Kawala, a spokesperson for the Kampala Metropolitan police, said he was found unconscious by ​passersby, who took him to a nearby hospital. He was ​transferred to another hospital, where he was pronounced dead on Wednesday.

Witnesses said attackers hit the footballer with paving stones before robbing him and fleeing, leaving him unconscious, the BBC reported.

Owori, 27, was a right-back and midfielder for SC Villa. He helped the team win a record 17th Uganda Premier League title in 2024.

He started his senior career in 2016 at the Uganda Premier League side Vipers Sports Club and had stints in Europe with Vélez CF in Spain and Utsiktens BK in Sweden.

He played for the national team in the qualifiers for the 2021 Africa Cup of Nations.

SC Villa said: “It is with profound sorrow that we announce the untimely passing of our captain, Owori, who had been receiving treatment at Case Clinic following an attack by suspected thugs. Our deepest condolences and prayers are with his family.”

The Federation ​of Uganda Football Associations said: “David was not just a footballer. He was ​both a leader and an inspiration to a generation. As ​Captain of SC Villa, he led with courage, humility and passion. In the Uganda Cranes jersey, he carried the hopes of a nation.”

It added: “We have lost a son, a leader and a star. His light on and off the pitch will never be forgotten.”

The Ugandan parliament observed a minute of silence in Owori’s honour on Wednesday.

In June Sydney Gongodyo, a Ugandan rugby international, ​died after a mob attacked him in Kampala, mistaking him for a thief, police said.

Uganda’s National Council of Sports said: “Sadly, ​Ugandan sport has been hit with many such ​tragedies lately, and we hope for justice and a lasting solution.”
